content.body: Imagine you need to save a binary tree to a file or send it over a network. How can you represent its structure as a simple string? In this lesson, you'll learn how to serialize and deserialize a binary tree—converting it to and from a string format while preserving its shape.
content.title: Introduction

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
1. Explain why serialization is needed for tree data structures.
2. Apply a traversal order to convert a tree into a string.
3. Implement both serialize and deserialize functions in JavaScript.
4. Handle empty nodes (null values) during the conversion process.
5. Reconstruct the original tree structure from the serialized string.
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Look at this simple binary tree with root value 1, left child 2, and right child 3. If you had to write it down as text to share with someone, how would you represent it? Think about what information you need to capture: values, structure, and empty spots.
content.title: Explore the tree
content.visualMetaphor: Show exploring from the root down branches; one level or one branch at a time.

content.body: You likely thought about listing values in some order and marking where branches end. This is the core challenge of serialization: capturing both values and structure in a linear format.
content.title: What you considered

content.body: With larger trees, simply listing values isn't enough—you need to preserve which node is whose child, and where branches are missing. Without a systematic approach, reconstructing the tree becomes impossible.
content.title: Why it gets complex

content.body: We can use tree traversal to explore branches from the root. By visiting nodes in a consistent order (like pre-order: root, left, right) and recording values—including null for empty branches—we create a complete blueprint. To deserialize, we replay the same traversal to rebuild the tree.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Use branch/root visual reasoning; visiting nodes or exploring levels one at a time.

content.body: We'll use depth-first pre-order traversal for both operations. During serialization, we visit each node, write its value, then recursively explore left and right branches—writing 'null' for empty ones. For deserialization, we read values in the same order, creating nodes and recursively building left and right subtrees.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Serialize: Perform pre-order traversal, appending node values (or 'null') to an array, then join into a string.
2. Deserialize: Split the string back into an array, then recursively consume values to reconstruct nodes and their children.
3. Base case: When we encounter 'null', return null (empty branch).
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the TreeNode class
steps.instruction: First, we need a basic TreeNode class to represent each node in our binary tree. Create the class with constructor that initializes val, left, and right properties.
steps.hint: The constructor should take a value parameter and set left/right to null by default.
steps.expectedOutcome: A TreeNode class that can be instantiated with a value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the foundation for our tree structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check that your constructor properly sets this.val, this.left, and this.right.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: class TreeNode { constructor(val) { this.val = val; this.left = null; this.right = null; } }

steps.title: Start the serialize function
steps.instruction: Create the serialize function that takes a root node. For now, just set up an empty array to collect values and define an inner helper function for traversal.
steps.hint: The function should return a string eventually, but first focus on structure.
steps.expectedOutcome: A serialize function with an empty array and a placeholder helper.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Good setup! Now we're ready to implement traversal.
steps.feedbackPartial: Make sure you declare an array variable inside serialize.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: function serialize(root) { const result = []; function traverse(node) {}; return ''; }

steps.title: Implement pre-order traversal for serialization
steps.instruction: Inside the helper function, implement pre-order traversal: if node is null, push 'null' to result; otherwise, push node.val, then recursively call traverse on node.left and node.right. Finally, call traverse(root) and return result joined by commas.
steps.hint: Remember the base case: empty tree (null root) should still be handled.
steps.expectedOutcome: A complete serialize function that converts tree to comma-separated string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You're capturing both values and structure with null markers.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check your if-else logic and recursive calls to traverse left and right.
steps.feedbackWrong: The traverse function should be: if (node === null) { result.push('null'); } else { result.push(node.val); traverse(node.left); traverse(node.right); }

steps.title: Start the deserialize function
steps.instruction: Create the deserialize function that takes a string. Split it by commas into an array, then set up an index to track current position. Define a helper function to build nodes recursively.
steps.hint: We'll consume values from the array one by one as we rebuild the tree.
steps.expectedOutcome: A deserialize function that splits the string and has a helper.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect setup! Now we can reconstruct nodes.
steps.feedbackPartial: Don't forget to split the data string and initialize an index.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: function deserialize(data) { const vals = data.split(','); let i = 0; function build() {}; return build(); }

steps.title: Implement node reconstruction
steps.instruction: In the build helper: get current value from array using index i. If it's 'null', increment i and return null. Otherwise, create a new TreeNode with the value (converted to number), increment i, set its left by recursively calling build(), then set its right similarly. Return the node.
steps.hint: The order of operations matters: create node, then build left subtree, then build right subtree.
steps.expectedOutcome: A complete deserialize function that reconstructs the tree from string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Well done! You're rebuilding the tree by replaying the traversal.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check value conversion and the recursive calls for left and right.
steps.feedbackWrong: The build function should be: const val = vals[i]; i++; if (val === 'null') return null; const node = new TreeNode(Number(val)); node.left = build(); node.right = build(); return node;

steps.title: Test the complete solution
steps.instruction: Create a small test tree, serialize it, then deserialize the result. Verify that the original and reconstructed trees match by checking their structure.
steps.hint: You can compare serialized strings or manually check a few node values.
steps.expectedOutcome: A working test that shows serialization and deserialize produce equivalent trees.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Your solution correctly round-trips the tree.
steps.feedbackPartial: Make sure your test creates a non-trivial tree and checks values.
steps.feedbackWrong: The test should create a tree, serialize it, deserialize, and verify key values match.

content.body: Congratulations! You've implemented tree serialization and deserialize using pre-order traversal. Remember: serialization records values and null markers in a specific order; deserialize replays that order to rebuild the tree. This pattern works because tree traversal creates a deterministic blueprint of the structure.
content.title: Done
